cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Destructive testing damages or destroys the test specimen: tensile testing, impact testing, fatigue testing and hardness testing.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Non-destructive testing (NDT) evaluates components without damage: visual inspection, ultrasonic, X-ray, dye penetrant and magnetic particle testing.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Tensile testing stretches a specimen to failure, measuring yield strength, UTS, ductility (elongation) and elastic modulus.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Hardness testing presses an indenter into the surface: Brinell (ball), Vickers (diamond pyramid), Rockwell (ball or cone).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Impact testing measures toughness: Charpy and Izod tests strike a notched specimen with a pendulum and record absorbed energy.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Fatigue testing subjects a specimen to repeated cyclic loading to determine the number of cycles to failure at given stress levels.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Visual inspection is the simplest NDT method: checking for surface cracks, corrosion, weld defects and dimensional accuracy.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Ultrasonic testing sends high-frequency sound waves into a material; reflections from defects are displayed on a screen.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: X-ray radiography produces images showing internal defects such as porosity, inclusions and cracks in welds and castings.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Dye penetrant testing applies a coloured or fluorescent liquid to the surface; it seeps into surface-breaking cracks, making them visible.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Quality control ensures products meet specifications: dimensional checks, material certificates, process monitoring and statistical sampling.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Testing Methods
cards.back: Tolerances define the acceptable range of variation: bilateral (+/-0.1 mm) or unilateral (0 to +0.2 mm).

cards.front: What should you know about gcse engineering exam tips — testing methods?
cards.back: 1. For Testing Methods questions, use precise design and technology terminology 2. Consider function, aesthetics, ergonomics, sustainability and cost in your answers 3. When evaluating, justify your design decisions with reference to user needs and specifications 4. Show your understanding of Testing Methods through both theory and practical application 5. Reference real products and manufacturing processes where relevant
